In particular, there is little work on scaling list ranking to large machines and input sizes. We reconsider list ranking starting from the ground-breaking results of Sibeyn a quarter century ago. We employ algorithm and performance engineering to improve his sparse ruling-set algorithm, making it capable of scaling to many processors, and provide a more detailed analysis of the impact of the algorithm's parameters, further guiding our practical implementation. We perform an extensive experimental study across a variety of input instances with different structural properties. We demonstrate that indirect communication, exploiting input locality, and message coalescing allows scaling to billions of elements on up to 24,576 cores.

papers.title: EP-NCO: Latency-Aware Service Placement using Neural Combinatorial Optimisers for Edge-Cloud Systems
papers.summary: Latency-sensitive Internet of Things (IoT) applications are increasingly deployed as interdependent microservices across heterogeneous edge-cloud infrastructures. Placing them under resource and network constraints is an NP-hard combinatorial optimisation problem. This study proposes EP-NCO, a graph-based neural combinatorial optimisation framework for service placement in compute continuum platforms. The objective accounts for execution latency, direct-link communication delay, and an approximate sharing of bandwidth among dependency flows that coexist in the resulting placement. Across held-out graph sizes generated by the same synthetic framework, the EP-NCO variant trained on Large instances with hard decoding achieved the lowest mean aggregate latency cost at every scale. It was 6.0%-12.5% lower than a genetic algorithm (GA), 14.4%-20.8% lower than particle swarm optimisation (PSO), and 1.2%-9.4% lower than the strongest reinforcement learning ablation. On Small instances, its mean cost was 10.5% below the best Gurobi solutions found and close to Gurobi's mean lower bound. The observed inference time of the EP-NCO variants was 0.88-1.03 s per instance, compared with 85-97 s for GA and PSO. As a result, the one-off training cost of the EP-NCO variant trained on Large instances with hard decoding is recovered after roughly 1,000 placements.

papers.title: Multiobjective Preexpectation Reasoning for Probabilistic Programs
papers.summary: Probabilistic programs with nondeterminism model planning problems in which a strategy typically resolves the nondeterminism to meet a specification. We study the multiobjective setting, meeting several specifications at once along a Pareto front, and provide a deductive, program-level account of strategy synthesis. Its core is a multiobjective preexpectation transformer mapping a tuple of postexpectations to the set of simultaneously achievable values, an element of the convex Hoare powerdomain. It conservatively extends weakest preexpectations and lifts standard loop rules. We develop rules to synthesize witnessing strategies as mixed determinizations that solve nondeterminism probabilistically. We prove the transformer and synthesis rules sound against an operational Markov decision process (MDP) semantics, without requiring a finite state space: our approach can be seen as a symbolic approach - at program level - for multiobjective optimization over infinite MDPs. We demonstrate our machinery using two case studies.

papers.title: Carbon-aware Resource Management for Latency-Sensitive Cloud Computing Environments: A Taxonomy and Future Directions
papers.summary: The proliferation of cloud-based latency-sensitive workloads, such as autonomous driving, real-time healthcare services, industrial automation, immersive interactive services, and intelligent AI-based applications requires infrastructures tuned to meet stringent latency constraints. Today, these workloads are reshaping the cloud from a general-purpose computing platform into a diverse ecosystem of workload-specific cloud environments. As demand for latency-sensitive workloads grows, cloud providers must scale their infrastructures accordingly, adversely increasing the carbon footprint and challenging net-zero goals. However, the strict performance requirements and rigid deployment patterns used to satisfy latency Service Level Objectives (SLOs) constrains conventional carbon optimization. Therefore, novel carbon-aware techniques are needed to exploit application-specific opportunities for reducing both operational and embodied carbon footprints while preserving latency guarantees. This survey examines carbon-aware resource management for latency-sensitive cloud computing environments. We introduce a holistic taxonomy that organizes existing techniques by carbon management objective, workload management mechanism, control architecture, system tier, latency requirements, and deployment stage. Then, we use this taxonomy to classify and critically analyze existing approaches, revealing the interactions and trade-offs between latency guarantees and operational and embodied carbon reduction. Finally, we identify limitations in the literature and present a structured research agenda for the design of sustainable latency-sensitive cloud systems.

papers.title: A Multi-Engine Dataflow for MoE Decoding on AWS Tranium
papers.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) decoding on scratchpad-based tensor accelerators (STA) is dominated by moving expert weights while the compute engines sit idle. This traffic is hard to hide, because the experts are known only after routing, and hard to shrink without losing quality or adding critical-path work. We present CARDAN, which represents each expert-weight matrix as a vector-quantized component plus a shared-basis low-rank component and co-designs this representation with a multi-engine decoding dataflow. The representation separates expert-common from expert-private work, so the dataflow overlaps DMA with computation on several engines. Across five MoE families on AWS Trainium3, CARDAN matches or improves BF16-teacher perplexity across all five models and speeds up batch-one decoding by 1.15-1.31x over AWS dense MoE megakernels, rising to 1.7x at batch size 16.

papers.title: MCCL: Measurement-based Collective Communication Library
papers.summary: Collective communication is a critical performance bottleneck in large-scale distributed training. Existing libraries and synthesis frameworks compute open-loop schedules once, assuming a static topology and peak link capacities. In production, however, persistent gray failures can silently degrade link throughput and latency for hours, causing pre-computed schedules to lose much of their efficiency during execution. In this paper, we present Measurement-based Collective Communication Library (MCCL), a collective communication library that closes the loop between runtime network measurement and dynamic schedule synthesis. MCCL passively measures GPU-to-GPU throughput, detects persistent degradation, re-synthesizes the affected communication-intensive schedules with warm-started synthesizers, and hot-swaps them without interrupting training. We validate the complete loop on a multi-node hardware prototype and use simulations to evaluate cluster-scale scenarios. In our experiments, MCCL incurs negligible overhead (<2%) while maintaining high measurement accuracy (<1.2% error) and low schedule hot-swap time (about 12 ms). Notably, under gray failures, MCCL reduces training time by up to 4.99x over static schedules on simulated training workloads for state-of-the-art LLMs such as Llama and DeepSeek.

papers.title: Structure-Aware Equivalence for Evaluating Autoformalized Statements
papers.summary: Evaluating autoformalized mathematical statements requires determining whether a candidate preserves the mathematical claim intended by a trusted reference. Existing methods approach this problem from complementary directions: reference-free learned evaluators estimate semantic agreement but are not constrained to a formal equivalence relation, while reference-based proof methods typically employ whole-statement logical equivalence to provide formal certificates, which is too coarse for translation fidelity and may identify mathematically unrelated statements. We introduce Structure-Aware Equivalence (SAE), a role-preserving formal equivalence relation between syntactic and whole-statement logical equivalence that allows formally justified reformulations while preserving translation-relevant mathematical structure. We operationalize SAE in the Autoformalization Correctness Evaluator (ACE), which provides certified equivalence or inequivalence judgments and reports Inconclusive otherwise. On ProofNetVerif, a benchmark introduced with BEq+, ACE retains substantial equivalent-case coverage while remaining highly conservative in certifying disputed or inequivalent pairs. On targeted diagnostics, BEq+ accepts 94-96% of unrelated but whole-statement logically equivalent pairs, while Mathesis LeanScorer accepts 42% of localized meaning-changing perturbations; ACE accepts none of either set as equivalent.

papers.title: M3D-FLOW: A Monolithic 3-D-Stackable Processing-Near-DRAM Architecture for Generative Normalizing Flow Applications
papers.summary: Normalizing Flows (NFs) have shown strong results in generative modeling, recently reaching state-of-the-art image generation performance. However, their repetitive, sequential operations limit the computational and memory efficiency achievable with GPUs and TPUs. We propose M3D-FLOW, a novel monolithic 3D-stackable (M3D) DRAM-based processing-near-memory (PNM) architecture that eliminates memory bottlenecks using a Cu-Cu hybrid-bonded logic die integrated with an M3D DRAM die. The M3D DRAM provides dense bank integration and a tiered organization with variable access latencies that M3D-FLOW exploits for the efficient processing of different NF workloads. To maximize compute density while minimizing area, energy, and thermal overhead, M3D-FLOW employs hybrid binary--stochastic floating-point multipliers, performing mantissa multiplication in the stochastic domain and exponent operations in the binary domain. A pipelined execution strategy maps sequential NF stages across dynamically partitioned PE groups, and together with the stochastic hardware, enables M3D-FLOW to achieve at least $6.6\times$ higher performance and $3\times$ better energy efficiency than prior PNM accelerators, with only a 2.2% bits-per-dimension (BPD) increase over bfloat16 and 4.1% over FP32. An analysis of stochastic hardware variants further shows that shorter stochastic bitstreams reduce execution time by up to $3.3\times$ at the cost of higher approximation error, providing a concrete design guide for latency--accuracy trade-offs.

papers.title: Weight Placement Is Not Enough: Synchronization in Multi-Node CPU Decoding of Ternary LLMs
papers.summary: Ternary LLMs read only a few gigabytes per decoded token, yet on dual-socket servers with four NUMA nodes the fastest ternary runtime we found uses less than half of the memory bandwidth. Placing each weight on the node of the thread that reads it is necessary but not enough: in a decode engine with node-local weights that reuses ik_llama's kernels, threads on two generations of Xeon servers still spend 20-48% of each token waiting at synchronization points. Per-thread barrier traces show that most of the wait is for the slowest threads of each node; the barriers' own latency (microseconds each, but up to 12% of the token for the smallest model) and serial per-node work are smaller parts. On identical kernels, a Megatron-style column split beats a row-owned split without cross-node reductions in every configuration we measured, and isolating the number of barriers shows that most of its gain comes from its threads waiting less for each other and for their node leaders, and only a minority from having fewer barriers. Where decoding is DRAM-bound, the resulting engine is 1.5-2.1x faster than ik_llama with all cores and 1.5-1.9x faster than ik_llama at its fastest thread count (3.2x and 2.8x for a small model that runs from the L3 cache), at the same accuracy and with less energy per token.

papers.title: A parity obstruction to degree-optimal syndrome extraction in bivariate bicycle codes
papers.summary: Syndrome extraction for a CSS code has depth at least the Tanner-graph degree $\Delta$, attained by edge colouring if gate order is ignored; correctness adds a parity constraint. We prove three general obstructions to depth-$\Delta$ extraction and show that, for every two-block group-algebra code with weight-three polynomials whose checks overlap in at most two qubits, no correct single-round circuit with one ancilla per check and one CNOT per Tanner edge has depth six: the minimum is seven, so the seven-layer cycle of Bravyi \emph{et al.} is optimal for their seven bivariate bicycle codes. This is the first analytic, family-wide impossibility result, extending prior instance-specific solver-based infeasibility results. The hypothesis cannot be dropped: a single orbit of four-qubit overlaps with a collision element of even order and $2$-height at most eight makes depth six attainable, and a $[[72,8,6]]$ code of this kind has a verified six-layer circuit. The refutations carry DRAT certificates.

papers.title: MockingBird: Context-aware Repository-level Code Translation with Isolated Validation
papers.summary: Despite advances in repository-level code translation, automated type resolution across differing type systems and translation validation (functional-equivalence checking) remain challenging. This paper proposes MockingBird, combining context-aware type resolution with mock-based isolated validation. MockingBird retrieves API documentation and contextual code information per source-language type, prompting an LLM to resolve precise cross-language type mappings, reducing the manual effort of existing approaches. Using this automatically constructed type map, MockingBird employs custom serialization/deserialization to generate equivalent target-language mock objects, validating each translation unit in isolation without test translation, eliminating test-overfitting risks and translation challenges. On 10 Java-to-Python tasks from the AlphaTrans benchmark, MockingBird improves functional equivalence from the state-of-the-art 25.14% to 43.10%, with no manual type-mapping correction needed. A 700-fragment study shows MockingBird achieves 0 false positives and 0.9% false negatives, substantially outperforming GraalVM (2.4% false positives, 7.6% false negatives) and MatchFixAgent (11.0% combined mislabel rate). The pipeline is also LLM-agnostic, maintaining these gains with both DeepSeekCoder-33B and the smaller Devstral-24B.

papers.title: From Fuzzy to Exact: The Halo Architecture for Infinite-Depth Reasoning via Rational Arithmetic
papers.summary: The prevailing scaling paradigm of Large Language Models (LLMs) rests on a substrate of "Fuzzy" floating-point arithmetic. To mitigate the inherent instability of this approximate foundation, modern architectures have erected a complex scaffolding of structural and numerical heuristics--Complex Residuals, Pre-RMSNorm, Attention Scaling, and Gradient Clipping--consuming significant compute solely to prevent numerical collapse. We propose a paradigm shift to the "Exact". We introduce the Halo Architecture, grounded in the Rational Field (Q) and powered by a custom Exact Inference Unit (EIU). To resolve the exponential bit-width growth of rational arithmetic, Halo employs a Dual-Ring Topology that unifies two complementary control mechanisms: (1) The Micro-Ring (Continuum Maintenance), which strictly bounds memory complexity via Diophantine Approximation; and (2) The Macro-Ring (Symbolic Alignment), which enforces logical consistency via periodic state collapse. This stable dual-ring substrate allows for the "Great Dismantling" of numerical scaffolding, reducing the Transformer block to its "Clean" algebraic form (Tabula Rasa). Furthermore, we verify the "Efficiency Paradox": the elimination of gradient noise (sigma -> 0) allows for Macro-Learning Rates, potentially reducing the Total Time-to-Convergence by orders of magnitude. Halo demonstrates that General Intelligence requires the hybridization of continuous fields and discrete chains under a rigorous mathematical framework.

papers.title: Sharing is caring: Attestable and Trusted Workflows out of Distrustful Components
papers.summary: Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) protect private memory and attest initial code and configuration, but neither constrain nor attest shared channels between TEEs or with the untrusted host. Confidentiality thus depends on the functional correctness of all in-TEE code accessing these channels: a single misuse can leak data and compromise a pipeline. This assumption is increasingly untenable for agentic applications that generate code at runtime and cloud pipelines of mutually distrustful components. We present MICA, a confidential-computing firmware extension that decouples confidentiality from trust in in-TEE code. MICA lets tenants define, restrict, and attest channel constraints between TEEs and with the untrusted host, including transitive constraints spanning a pipeline. It extends attestation to groups of communicating TEEs, letting external parties verify the confidentiality properties induced by these constraints across a pipeline. We implement MICA on Arm CCA by extending the Realm Management Monitor with a small policy language, requiring no hardware changes and minor QEMU and KVM changes. Our evaluation demonstrates support for confidential agentic applications and pipeline computations without trusting the functional correctness of in-TEE code. MICA increases the TCB by 7% and incurs infrequent setup costs: 2-4% boot-time overhead, approximately 1.5 s for policy upload, and 246-598 ms for group attestation. Once established, Realm communication is direct, uses protected memory, and requires no MICA intervention or software encryption, yielding up to 14.5 times lower cross-TEE message latency than encrypted communication over untrusted memory.

papers.title: ACHEM: A Real-Time Digital Twin Framework with Channel and Radio Emulation
papers.summary: Digital twins are becoming an important tool for designing, developing, testing, and optimizing next-generation wireless communication systems. Over the past decade, system softwarization has become a reality, and wireless communication systems are no exception. Software-Defined Radios (SDRs), in general, and Universal Software Radio Peripherals (USRPs), in particular, are often used for prototyping and testing advanced wireless systems. Unfortunately, there is currently no end-to-end, software-based, general-purpose testing environment for SDR-based systems: developers often rely on benchtop setups or even small testbeds, but those are costly and cumbersome to build. At the other end of the spectrum, simulations often rely on simplified channel/radio models and typically do not execute full-stack production code, which can increase development effort and reduce fidelity. In this paper, we propose ACHEM (A Channel Emulator), the first software-based, end-to-end wireless channel emulation environment and toolset for communication systems based on SDRs, specifically USRPs. With the proposed emulator and toolkit, any USRP-based system can be fully emulated at the I/Q level in a pure digital environment without requiring specialized hardware (e.g., vehicles, USRPs, FPGAs, or GPUs). The proposed emulator supports multiple transmitters and receivers, MIMO communications, multiple frequencies, heterogeneous sampling rates, real-time node mobility through vehicle emulation, antenna radiation patterns, and various channel models. ACHEM facilitates wireless digital twin development and deployment. ACHEM is validated with several popular open-source USRP-based wireless communication applications, including GNU Radio, srsRAN 4G/5G, and OpenAirInterface.

papers.title: Quantifying and Defending against the Privacy Risk in Logit-based Federated Learning
papers.summary: Federated learning aims to protect data privacy by collaboratively learning a model without sharing private data among clients. Unlike traditional parameter-based FL methods that exchange model weights or gradients during training, emerging logit-based FL approaches share model outputs (logits) on public data. This strategy promotes model heterogeneity, reduces communication overhead, and enhances clients' privacy. However, the potential privacy risks associated with these logit-based methods have been largely overlooked. This research presents the first theoretical and empirical analysis of a hidden privacy risk in logit-based FL methods - the risk that a semi-honest server (adversary) may learn clients' private models from logits. To quantify and address this threat, we develop the Adaptive Model Stealing Attack (AdaMSA) by leveraging historical logits during training. Notably, we observe that this inherent privacy risk persists even when public data is unrelated to private data, emphasizing the urgency to address privacy vulnerabilities in logit-based FL methods. Moreover, our theoretical analysis establishes the bounds of this privacy risk. We then propose a simple but effective defense strategy that perturbs the transmitted logits in the direction that minimizes the privacy risk while maximally preserving the training performance. We further provide a theoretical analysis of FedLP's privacy and utility properties. The experimental results validate our analysis and demonstrate the effectiveness of AdaMSA and our defense strategy.

papers.title: SeFoRA: Sketch-Aggregated Federated Low-Rank Adaptation with Heterogeneous Client Ranks
papers.summary: We consider federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning of foundation models, e.g., LLMs and LVMs, using low-rank adaptation (LoRA; ~Hu et al.\ 2022). Combining LoRA with federated learning introduces challenges absent from either setting alone: clients may use different LoRA ranks, making their factor matrices dimension-incompatible, and factor-wise averaging suffers from a bilinear mismatch. We propose SeFoRA, a sketch-aggregated federated LoRA algorithm in which each client transmits a linear sketch of its local $\Delta \mathbf{W}$ updates, enabling direct aggregation at the federator. As a result, SeFoRA overcomes the rank heterogeneity challenge and alleviates the bilinear mismatch. We establish convergence to a neighborhood of a first-order stationary point at rate $\\mathcal{O}(T^{-1/2})$. Extensive numerical experiments on language and vision models showcase the performance of our algorithm compared to existing methods.

papers.title: XIR: A Framework for Interoperability across Cross-Chain Protocols Based on a Verifiable Intermediate Representation
papers.summary: Cross-chain protocols enable applications to exchange messages across blockchains. Under point-to-point configurations, communication depends on a direct connection between the source and destination blockchains, limiting blockchain reachability and requiring additional configurations to connect more blockchains. To quantify this problem, this paper analyzes approximately 25 million mainnet cross-chain transaction events collected from six protocols (Axelar, CCIP, Hyperlane, LayerZero, Relay, and Wormhole) between January and October 2025. The resulting graph covers 286 active blockchains and 11,935 directly connected ordered blockchain pairs. These connections provide a direct reachability of 14.64%, while full direct connectivity would require 81,510 point-to-point configurations. We present XIR, a framework for interoperability across cross-chain protocols based on a verifiable intermediate representation. This representation binds an application message to an ordered record of authenticated cross-chain protocol deliveries, preserving message identity and verification history across protocol boundaries. XIR Gateways and XIR Adapters use this representation to compose existing connections into same-protocol and cross-protocol multi-hop paths. We implement an XIR prototype integrating Hyperlane and LayerZero and evaluate it in local and public-testnet environments. Theoretical analysis and evaluation show that, with correctly configured cross-chain protocol connections, XIR avoids 67,018 additional point-to-point configurations, equivalent to 84.88% of the total required by a point-to-point configuration baseline serving the same reachable pairs, and increases reachability from 14.64% to 96.86% of all ordered blockchain pairs.
